chapters.title: The House of Lac
chapters.subtitle: Varanavata, a festival town and a palace built to burn
narrative: Duryodhana's agent Purochana builds a fine residence for the Pandavas at Varanavata out of lac, resin and other things that burn easily. Before they leave Hastinapura, Vidura warns Yudhishthira in a riddling speech only he understands, about a fire that does not burn the creature that shelters underground. Later Vidura sends a trusted miner who digs a tunnel beneath the house in secret.

For a year the Pandavas live there, hunting by day and sleeping on their guard. On the night they choose, Kunti holds a feast. A Nishada woman and her five sons, who had come for food, drink deeply and fall asleep inside. Bhima sets the house alight, Purochana dies in the fire, and the Pandavas and their mother escape through the tunnel to the Ganga, where a boat sent by Vidura carries them across.

In the ashes the people of Varanavata find Purochana and the bodies of a woman and five young men, whom they take for Kunti and her sons, and Hastinapura believes the Pandavas are dead. Dhritarashtra mourns publicly and Bhishma grieves; Vidura, who knows the truth, says little. The epic records the deaths of the Nishada woman and her sons almost in passing, and modern readers have often stopped there to ask what the Pandavas' survival cost others.

story_context.sources_note: The episode is told in the Jatugriha (lac house) section of the Adi Parva. Whether the Pandavas knowingly let the Nishada family die, or simply took advantage of their deaths, is debated; the text's brevity leaves room for both readings. Vidura's warning is described as spoken in a language or idiom unfamiliar to others, and translators render it differently.

chapters.title: Draupadi's Swayamvara
chapters.subtitle: A great bow, a target set high, and a choice that redrew the map of kingdoms
narrative: Drupada of Panchala had not forgotten the day Drona's pupils bound him and carried him before his old schoolfellow. As the epic tells it, he performed a sacrifice to obtain a son who would kill Drona, and from the fire rose Dhrishtadyumna and then a dark, radiant daughter: Draupadi, also called Krishnaa and Yajnaseni, 'born of the sacrifice'. Drupada had always hoped to give her to Arjuna. Believing, like everyone else, that the Pandavas might have died at Varanavata, he set a test he thought only Arjuna could pass: a massive bow, and a target placed high above a mechanical device, to be struck through its opening.

Kings came from every quarter, and one after another they failed even to string the bow. Among the Brahmins in the crowd sat five brothers in disguise, newly arrived from Ekachakra with their mother. One of them rose, strung the bow in a moment and brought the target down. The princes protested that a Brahmin had carried off a kshatriya's prize; Bhima and Arjuna held them back, and Krishna, who had recognised the brothers, helped calm the quarrel.

What happened when Karna stepped forward depends on which Mahabharata you read. In the widely known vulgate text, Draupadi refuses before he can shoot, declaring she will not choose a charioteer's son. The Critical Edition prepared at Pune omits that refusal; in its text Karna does not win her either, and he is usually read as one more warrior who could not complete the feat. Which reading is older is still argued over. Popular retellings add their own details too, such as a fish target aimed at only through its reflection in water, which is not how the Critical Edition describes the contest.

At the potter's house where they lodged, the brothers called out to Kunti that they had brought home alms. Without looking, she told them to share it among themselves. Then she saw Draupadi. The marriage of one woman to five husbands troubled Drupada and, the epic admits, needed defending: Yudhishthira reasons from what he sees in his brothers' faces, and Vyasa answers with stories of Draupadi's earlier birth. A bride won by one archer became the bond tying the Pandavas to Panchala, and soon to Krishna.

story_context.sources_note: Karna's attempt differs by recension: the vulgate has Draupadi reject him as a suta's son, while the Critical Edition omits the rejection, leaving Karna as one more suitor who does not succeed; how much of his attempt belongs to the oldest text is debated. The fish-and-reflection target is a feature of later and regional retellings. Vyasa's justifications of the shared marriage (Draupadi's earlier life, the story of the five Indras) are part of the epic's own text, but their meaning remains much debated.

The outcome bound the Pandavas to Panchala and, through Krishna, to the Yadavas.

chapters.title: The Birth of Indraprastha
chapters.subtitle: A city raised from a wilderness, and the rules meant to keep it whole
narrative: News that the Pandavas lived, and were now allied to Panchala, reached Hastinapura. In Dhritarashtra's council Bhishma, Drona and Vidura urged that the brothers receive their share of the kingdom; Duryodhana wanted them weakened by intrigue, and Karna argued for open force while they were still few. Vidura was sent to bring them home, and Dhritarashtra divided the realm. The Pandavas' half was Khandavaprastha, a wild, forested tract beside the Yamuna, far from the comforts of the old capital.

There they built a city: walls and moats, gates and gardens, and a population of merchants, artisans and learned people drawn to a young king known for his fairness. They named it Indraprastha. Some later retellings credit divine architects with its building; the older narrative is more interested in what the city stood for than in how its towers rose.

The sage Narada came to warn them. He told the story of Sunda and Upasunda, asura brothers who shared everything until desire for one woman turned them against each other. The Pandavas agreed on a rule: whoever intruded on a brother alone with Draupadi would go into exile. Soon a Brahmin begged for help recovering stolen cattle, and Arjuna's weapons lay in the room where Yudhishthira sat with Draupadi. Arjuna chose the Brahmin, kept the rule against his brother's pleading, and left.

His wanderings brought him three marriages: to the Naga princess Ulupi, to Chitrangada of Manipura, and to Subhadra, Krishna's sister, whom he carried off on Krishna's own advice while Balarama raged. Subhadra arrived at Indraprastha dressed as a cowherd woman to greet Draupadi, and in time bore Abhimanyu. The kingdom flourished. But on its edge the Khandava forest still stood, and it had inhabitants of its own.

story_context.sources_note: The length of Arjuna's exile (traditionally twelve years) and how his marriages fit a vow of celibacy were discussed by commentators; the text has Ulupi argue that saving her life outweighs the vow. Divine builders of Indraprastha appear mainly in later and regional retellings.

chapters.title: The Burning of Khandava
chapters.subtitle: Gifts of fire, and grudges that outlive a generation
narrative: Krishna and Arjuna had gone to the banks of the Yamuna near Indraprastha when a tall Brahmin, blazing like the sun, came to ask them for food. He was Agni, the fire god, and the food he wanted was the Khandava forest. He had tried before to consume it, but Indra protected the forest for the sake of his friend Takshaka, the Naga who lived there, and put out every attempt with rain. To make the heroes equal to Indra, Agni asked Varuna for gifts: Arjuna received the bow Gandiva, two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot bearing a monkey banner; Krishna received a discus, given in the text by Agni himself, and from Varuna the mace Kaumodaki.

The epic describes the burning without softening it. Krishna and Arjuna drove round the forest on two sides while it burned, and turned back the creatures that tried to escape. When Indra's clouds gathered, Arjuna's arrows formed a canopy that held off the rain, and the gods who came to fight eventually withdrew, told by a voice that Takshaka was not even in the forest. Many modern readers find the episode troubling, and some read it as a memory of land being cleared for farming. Those readings are interpretations; the text presents it as a heroic feat that pleased Agni.

A few survived. Maya, an asura architect, ran to Arjuna for protection, and Krishna lowered his discus; in gratitude Maya would build the Pandavas an assembly hall like no other. Takshaka's son Ashvasena escaped. The Nagas come back at decisive moments: Ashvasena seeks Arjuna at Kurukshetra, and Takshaka, the forest's absent lord, later causes the death of Arjuna's grandson Parikshit. That death leads Janamejaya to the snake sacrifice where the Mahabharata is first recited.

story_context.sources_note: The episode is in the Critical Edition and closes the Adi Parva. Explanations of Agni's illness, the number of his failed attempts and the lists of creatures vary between manuscripts and retellings. Ecological and land-clearing readings are modern interpretations. Takshaka's killing of Parikshit is set off in the text by a sage's curse, so the link back to Khandava is thematic rather than a stated motive.

chapters.title: The Rajasuya Assembly
chapters.subtitle: A king of kings is consecrated, and the first honour starts a quarrel
narrative: Maya kept his word and built the Pandavas an assembly hall full of illusions: pools that looked like solid floor, crystal floors that looked like water. In it the sage Narada described the halls of the gods and brought a message from Pandu, who wished his son to perform the Rajasuya, the royal consecration that proclaims one king paramount over others. Yudhishthira turned to Krishna, and Krishna named the obstacle: Jarasandha of Magadha, who held many captive kings he meant to sacrifice, and whose attacks had already driven the Yadavas from Mathura to Dwaraka.

Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna entered Jarasandha's capital, Girivraja, dressed as snataka Brahmins, and challenged him to single combat. Jarasandha chose Bhima. The text has them wrestle for nearly two weeks before Bhima killed him, and the captive kings were freed and Jarasandha's son placed on the throne. Then the four younger brothers went out in the four directions, conquering or securing the submission of kingdoms and bringing back tribute.

At the sacrifice, with Vyasa among the officiating priests, Bhishma advised that the first honour go to Krishna, and Sahadeva offered it. Shishupala of Chedi refused to accept this: Krishna was not a king, he said, and the Pandavas had insulted every ruler present. His abuse grew. Bhishma told how Krishna had promised Shishupala's mother to forgive him a hundred offences, and when that limit was passed Krishna released his discus. The epic says that a radiance rose from the fallen king and entered Krishna.

Duryodhana stayed on after the guests left and walked through Maya's hall. He mistook a crystal floor for a pool, and then a real pool for floor and fell in, and Bhima laughed, and the attendants with him. In popular retellings Draupadi mocks him as 'the blind man's son'; that line is not found in the Critical Edition, though Duryodhana's sense of humiliation and envy is central there. He went home burning, with Shakuni at his side.

The length of the Jarasandha duel, the number of captive kings and the lists of kingdoms in the digvijaya vary by manuscript. The radiance entering Krishna is read devotionally (as liberation) and also critically.

chapters.title: The Dice Hall
chapters.subtitle: A game in which a kingdom, five brothers and a queen are staked
narrative: Duryodhana came home from Indraprastha sick with envy. His uncle Shakuni had a plan: invite Yudhishthira to a game of dice, at which Shakuni was a master. Dhritarashtra hesitated, Vidura warned that the game would destroy the family, and the blind king agreed anyway and had a new hall built. Vidura himself was sent with the invitation. Yudhishthira saw the danger, but said that he did not refuse a challenge once it was made, and he came. When Duryodhana announced that Shakuni would throw the dice on his behalf, Yudhishthira objected that one should play for oneself, then accepted.

The epic slows down for the losses. Jewels, gold, chariots, servants, the army, the kingdom. Then the brothers, beginning with Nakula and Sahadeva, then Arjuna, then Bhima. Then Yudhishthira staked himself and lost. At Shakuni's prompting he staked Draupadi, and the dice fell against him again. Vidura protested that the game was ruinous. Most of the elders said nothing.

Duryodhana sent for Draupadi as a slave. She sent back a question: had Yudhishthira lost himself before he staked her? Dushasana dragged her into the hall by her hair, in a single garment. Vikarna, a younger Kaurava, argued that she had not been lawfully won; Karna shouted him down and ordered the Pandavas and Draupadi stripped. When Dushasana pulled at her garment, the text says more cloth kept appearing. The Critical Edition records this wonder without Draupadi's prayer to Krishna, which belongs to many other manuscripts and to most popular retellings. Bhima swore terrible vows against Dushasana and Duryodhana.

Jackals howled in the king's fire-sanctuary. Alarmed, and pressed by Gandhari and Vidura, Dhritarashtra offered Draupadi boons. She asked for Yudhishthira's freedom and then for the other four brothers with their weapons, and declined a third boon. The Pandavas left free. But Duryodhana persuaded his father to call them back for one more game, with a new stake: twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year in hiding. Yudhishthira returned, played and lost.

chapters.title: Draupadi's Question
chapters.subtitle: A question of law asked in a hall that had forgotten it
narrative: When the usher came to fetch her as a slave, Draupadi did not come. She sent him back with a question for the assembly: whom had Yudhishthira lost first, himself or her? If a man had already become another's property, what right did he have left to stake his wife? Duryodhana's answer was to send Dushasana, who dragged her into the hall by her hair, in a single garment, while she was in her monthly seclusion.

Standing before the elders, she asked again. Bhishma answered that the way of dharma was subtle, that a man without property could not stake what was not his, yet a wife remains subject to her husband, and that he could not decide. Vikarna, one of Dhritarashtra's own sons, argued that the wager was invalid: Yudhishthira had played in the grip of gambling, one of the recognised vices of kings; Draupadi was the wife of all five brothers, not his alone; he had staked her after losing himself; and Shakuni, not he, had first named her. Karna shouted him down, called Draupadi a woman with many husbands, and ordered the Pandavas and Draupadi stripped.

As Dushasana pulled at her garment, the text says that more cloth of the same kind kept appearing, until he sat down exhausted. Who protected her depends on the manuscript: the Critical Edition names no rescuer, while many other manuscripts and nearly all popular and devotional retellings have Draupadi call on Krishna, who answers. Bhima made his vows. Then omens filled the hall, and the blind king, afraid at last, offered Draupadi boons. Her question was never answered.

chapters.title: The Exile
chapters.subtitle: Twelve years in the forest, and what kingship could not teach
narrative: Vidura described the departure to the blind king: Yudhishthira walking with his face covered, Bhima looking at his own arms, Arjuna scattering sand, the twins smeared with dust, Draupadi weeping with her hair unbound, and the family priest Dhaumya chanting hymns for the dead. Kunti stayed behind in Vidura's house. Brahmins followed the exiles into the forest, and Yudhishthira, unable to feed them, prayed to the Sun, who in the epic gives him a vessel that provides food each day. Retellings describe the vessel and its rules in different ways.

In the Kamyaka and Dwaita forests the Pandavas learned what it was to have nothing to command. Bhima killed the rakshasa Kirmira. Krishna came, and Draupadi poured out her grief to him. She and Bhima pressed Yudhishthira hard: a king who forgives every wrong, they argued, abandons his duty; Draupadi went so far as to question the justice of the creator. Yudhishthira answered with a defence of patience and of keeping his word, and the epic gives both sides their full say. On Vyasa's advice Arjuna went alone to the Himalaya, fought a mysterious hunter who turned out to be Shiva, received the Pashupata weapon, and spent years in Indra's heaven learning the use of divine arms.

The forest was full of stories. The sage Brihadashva told Yudhishthira of Nala, another king who lost his kingdom at dice; Markandeya told of Rama's exile and of Savitri, who argued with Death for her husband's life. The brothers went on pilgrimage to sacred fords, and on a mountain path Bhima met Hanuman, his elder brother as a fellow son of the Wind. These embedded tales make up a large share of the Vana Parva, and they seem chosen to show the exiles their own situation from the outside.

Enemies did not leave them alone. Duryodhana came to the forest to show off his wealth, was captured by Gandharvas, and was freed by the Pandavas at Yudhishthira's insistence, a rescue more humiliating to him than defeat. Jayadratha tried to carry off Draupadi and was caught and spared. And Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, asked Karna for his natural armour and earrings, and Karna gave them.

chapters.title: The Yaksha's Questions
chapters.subtitle: A still lake, a voice and a final choice
narrative: Near the end of the forest years, a Brahmin came to the Pandavas in distress: a deer had carried off his fire-sticks on its antlers. The brothers gave chase deep into the Dwaita forest until thirst overcame them. Nakula climbed a tree, saw water, and went to fetch it. At the lake a voice, seemingly from a crane, told him to answer its questions before drinking. He drank and fell. Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima followed him, ignored the voice, and fell beside the water.

Yudhishthira came last and found his brothers lying still. He did not drink. He asked who spoke, and a towering Yaksha showed himself and put his questions: about the sun and the earth, about dharma, happiness, the path to follow and the nature of a person. Yudhishthira answered each in turn. Among the answers best remembered: a mother outweighs the earth and a father stands higher than the sky; and the greatest wonder is that every day people watch others die, yet those who remain live as if they never will.

Then the Yaksha offered to restore one brother. Yudhishthira passed over Bhima and Arjuna, the warriors he would need, and chose Nakula, so that Madri, like Kunti, would still have a living son. The Yaksha revealed himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira's divine father, restored all four, returned the fire-sticks and granted that the Pandavas would pass their thirteenth year unrecognised. The number, wording and order of the questions vary between manuscripts, and popular collections often add more.

chapters.title: The Kingdom of Virata
chapters.subtitle: A year lived under borrowed names
narrative: The thirteenth year asks for something harder than endurance: invisibility. By the terms of the dice game, if the Pandavas are recognised before it ends they must go back into the forest for another twelve years. So they wrap their weapons and hide them in a shami tree near a cremation ground, and walk into the court of King Virata of Matsya as strangers. Yudhishthira becomes Kanka, a brahmin who keeps the king company at dice; Bhima becomes Ballava the cook; Arjuna becomes Brihannala, a teacher of dance living as a eunuch; Nakula becomes Granthika among the horses, Sahadeva Tantipala among the herds; and Draupadi becomes Sairandhri, maid to Queen Sudeshna.

The masks cannot protect Draupadi from Kichaka, the queen's brother and commander of Virata's army. When he kicks her before the throne, the king does nothing, and Kanka, guarding the secret, sends her back to the women's quarters with a counsel of patience. It is Bhima who answers, meeting Kichaka at night in the dance hall. The year rhymes with the dice hall: once more a court watches a woman wronged, and once more the cost of restraint falls first on her.

As the year closes, the Trigartas strike Matsya from one side and the Kauravas raid its cattle from the other. Prince Uttara rides out boasting, with Brihannala as his charioteer, and panics at the sight of Bhishma, Drona and Karna. Arjuna puts the prince at the reins, takes the Gandiva back from the shami tree, and turns the Kuru host back from a single chariot. Whether the year had truly ended becomes the first quarrel of the coming war; in the epic Bhishma, counting the extra months of the lunar calendar, judges that it had.

chapters.title: Krishna's Peace Mission
chapters.subtitle: The last embassy before the war
narrative: Upaplavya, a town in Virata's kingdom, becomes the Pandavas' camp, and for a season the epic turns from arrows to words. Envoys travel back and forth: Drupada's priest to Hastinapura, Sanjaya from Dhritarashtra to the Pandavas. Yudhishthira's demand shrinks from the return of Indraprastha to, as he tells Sanjaya, a mere five villages. At last Krishna goes himself, saying that even if peace fails, no one should be able to claim it was never offered.

In Hastinapura he declines Duryodhana's feast and lodges with Vidura. He visits Kunti, who sends her sons the old story of Vidula, a mother who shamed her defeated son into rising again. In the Kuru assembly Krishna speaks, and Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and at last Gandhari plead with Duryodhana. His answer, in the epic's own image, is that he will not yield even as much land as the point of a needle would pierce. He walks out, and plots to seize the envoy.

The Udyoga Parva then has Krishna reveal a form filled with gods and heroes; the hall trembles, and nothing changes. As he leaves the city he takes Karna into his chariot and tells him the secret of his birth: he is Kunti's eldest son, elder brother to the Pandavas, and could be king. Karna refuses, out of loyalty to Duryodhana and to the charioteer's family who raised him, and in one of the epic's most haunting speeches imagines the coming war as a vast sacrifice. The embassy ends with every door closed.

chapters.title: Kunti and Karna
chapters.subtitle: A mother at the river, a son facing the sun
narrative: Each morning Karna stands at the river and prays facing east until the sun has warmed his back. The epic places Kunti there, waiting in the shade of her eldest son, the child she set adrift in a basket long ago before she was married. She has come too late, and she knows it.

She tells him what Krishna has already told him: that she is his mother, that the sun is his father, that the Pandavas are his brothers. In the epic a voice from the sun confirms her words. Karna answers with the grief of a lifetime: where was she when he was mocked as a charioteer's son? Adhiratha and Radha raised him; Duryodhana honoured him. He will not desert his friend on the eve of war.

Yet he gives her something. He will not kill Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula or Sahadeva, even if they fall into his power; only Arjuna will he seek. Whichever of them dies, she will still have five sons. Kunti embraces him and goes. Popular retellings add further promises — for instance that Karna will loose a certain serpent-weapon only once — which are not part of the Critical Edition's account.

chapters.title: Kurukshetra
chapters.subtitle: Eighteen armies on a sacred field
narrative: The epic calls it a field of dharma long before it becomes a field of war. Here the hosts gather: eleven akshauhinis for Duryodhana, seven for the Pandavas, figures the epic gives with ritual precision and which are better read as a measure of catastrophe than as a muster roll. Allegiance has been decided by kinship, marriage, debt and accident. Shalya, brother of Madri and uncle of the twins, marches to join the Pandavas, accepts a lavish welcome he thinks is theirs, discovers it was Duryodhana's, and is bound. Balarama refuses both sides and goes on pilgrimage; Rukmi offers himself to each and is turned away by both.

Before battle the commanders agree on rules: equals should fight equals, no one should strike a warrior who flees, surrenders or is disarmed, and charioteers, drummers and attendants are not to be targets. Bhishma takes command of the Kauravas, Dhrishtadyumna of the Pandavas. Karna, stung by Bhishma's low rating of him, lays down his weapons for as long as the old man commands.

Then, with conches about to sound, Yudhishthira steps down from his chariot, sets aside his armour and walks unarmed toward the enemy. Both armies wonder whether he is surrendering. He bows to Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Shalya and asks leave to fight them. Bhishma blesses him and confesses that a man is bound to whoever sustains him: the Kauravas have bound him with wealth, though his wishes are with the Pandavas. Walking back, Yudhishthira calls out to anyone who would change sides — and Yuyutsu, a son of Dhritarashtra by a maidservant, crosses the field.

The akshauhini figures and the composition of an akshauhini (given in the Adi Parva) are traditional literary numbers, not historical counts. Lists of allies and commanders vary slightly between recensions. In the Bhishma Parva, Yudhishthira's walk to his elders and Yuyutsu's crossing come after the Bhagavad Gita on the same morning; this voyage shows them here, before the Gita, for clarity. Kurukshetra is traditionally identified with the region around modern Kurukshetra in Haryana.

chapters.title: Krishna or His Army
chapters.subtitle: Two visitors at a sleeping man's bedside
narrative: This scene steps back in time, to the weeks before the peace mission, when both sides were gathering allies. Arjuna and Duryodhana arrive at Dwaraka on the same day to ask Krishna for help, and find him asleep. Duryodhana, arriving first, takes a seat at the head of the bed; Arjuna stands at its foot. When Krishna wakes, his eyes fall first on Arjuna.

Krishna offers a choice to them both: on one side a vast force of cowherd warriors, the Narayanas; on the other, himself alone, who will not take up weapons in the battle. Because he saw Arjuna first, and Arjuna is the younger, Arjuna chooses first — and chooses Krishna. Duryodhana leaves delighted with an army. He goes on to Balarama, who declines to fight for either side.

The episode is often told as a lesson in humility or in what truly counts as strength. The epic itself is plainer: it is a scene about alliances, in which Krishna stays formally even-handed while giving the Pandavas exactly what they wanted. It also sets up the role on which the next chapter turns. Krishna will be Arjuna's charioteer.

chapters.title: The Bhagavad Gita
chapters.subtitle: A dialogue in the space between two armies
narrative: On the first morning the conches sound — Bhishma's first, then Krishna's Panchajanya and Arjuna's Devadatta. Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive into the open ground between the armies so that he can see whom he must fight. Krishna halts the chariot before Bhishma and Drona. Arjuna looks across and sees grandfathers, teachers, uncles, cousins, sons and friends. His limbs fail, the Gandiva slips from his hand, and he sits down in the chariot and says he will not fight.

What follows is the Bhagavad Gita: in the Critical Edition, seven hundred verses in eighteen chapters, chapters 23 to 40 of the Bhishma Parva. Krishna's answer moves from the immediate to the ultimate — the self that is not born and does not die, the duty proper to one's own nature, action performed without craving for its fruits, the disciplines of knowledge and of devotion. At Arjuna's request he reveals his universal form and names himself Time, the destroyer of worlds, already at work on the warriors standing in the field.

At the end Arjuna says his confusion is gone and that he will do as he is told. The Gita reaches us through layers: Sanjaya relates it to the blind Dhritarashtra, and in the Bhishma Parva he does so only after Bhishma has already fallen. Scholars debate when it was composed and how it came to sit inside the epic, and its readers — from medieval commentators such as Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva to Tilak, Aurobindo and Gandhi — have drawn from it very different, sometimes opposing, lessons.

chapters.title: Sanjaya's Sight
chapters.subtitle: The blind king who would not watch
narrative: Before the battle begins, Vyasa comes to the blind king Dhritarashtra and offers him sight so that he can watch the war. Dhritarashtra refuses: he does not want to see his own kin slaughtered, though he wants to hear everything. So Vyasa grants divine vision to Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and counsellor — the power to see every part of the field, by day or night, and even what is hidden in the warriors' minds.

The Bhishma Parva then makes a startling choice of order. Ten days pass. Sanjaya returns from the field and announces that Bhishma has fallen. Only then does the grief-stricken king ask him to tell everything from the beginning — and so the Gita opens with Dhritarashtra's question about what his sons and the sons of Pandu did on the field of dharma.

Sanjaya sees all and can change nothing. The epic's whole frame works this way: Ugrashravas repeats what Vaishampayana recited to Janamejaya, as Vyasa composed it — stories within stories, each listener a little further from the event and a little closer to us.

chapters.title: Bhishma's Fall
chapters.subtitle: The vow-keeper on a bed of arrows
narrative: For ten days Bhishma commands the Kaurava host, and no one can bring him down. He fights for the throne he swore to serve, while his heart, as he has openly admitted, is with the Pandavas, and Duryodhana repeatedly accuses him of holding back. Twice Krishna, who had promised not to take up arms, leaps from Arjuna's chariot to rush at him. In the Critical Edition's account he seizes his discus on one day and his whip on another; many retellings show him lifting a chariot wheel, perhaps because the Sanskrit chakra can mean either. Each time Arjuna holds him back, and Bhishma welcomes death at Krishna's hands.

On the night of the ninth day the Pandavas go to their grandfather's tent and ask him, in effect, how he can be killed. He tells them: he will not raise his weapons against Shikhandi, who was born a woman — in the epic, the princess Amba reborn to bring about his death. On the tenth day Arjuna rides behind Shikhandi. Bhishma lowers his bow, and Arjuna's arrows find him; the epic has Bhishma say he knows these arrows are Arjuna's, not Shikhandi's.

He falls as the sun sinks, and the shafts hold his body above the ground. He asks for a pillow; Arjuna gives him three arrows. Bhishma, granted by his father the power to choose the hour of his death, resolves to wait for the sun's turn northward. The next morning, with both armies gathered around him, he asks for water; Arjuna looses an arrow into the earth and a stream rises to his lips. When the others have gone, Karna, who had refused to fight while Bhishma commanded, comes to his side, and the old man tells him he has always known whose son he is.

Shikhandi's identity — born female, raised as a son, and in the Udyoga Parva given male sex by the yaksha Sthunakarna — is read in many ways by traditions and modern scholars. Bhishma lies on the bed of arrows for some fifty-eight nights, according to the Anushasana Parva. In the Critical Edition the pillow of arrows is given on the evening of the fall, while the spring of water and Karna's visit follow on the next day; the voyage's shots compress these moments.

chapters.title: Drona and the War's Turning Point
chapters.subtitle: The teacher takes command, and the rules of war begin to break
narrative: When Bhishma fell on the tenth day, command of the Kaurava host passed to Drona, the teacher who had trained both sides in the same courtyard. Duryodhana asked him for one thing: take Yudhishthira alive. A captured king could be drawn back to the dice, and the war could be won without being fought to the end. To clear the way, the Samshaptakas, warriors sworn to conquer or die, challenged Arjuna and pulled him to the far edge of the field.

Drona's five days of command (days eleven to fifteen in the usual reckoning) are where the war's restraints come apart. On the thirteenth day Abhimanyu died inside the circular array. On the fourteenth Arjuna kept his vow to kill Jayadratha before sunset, and the fighting, unusually, ran on into the night. In the dark Karna spent the one-use weapon he had been keeping for Arjuna to stop Ghatotkacha, whose death the epic describes Krishna greeting with relief rather than grief.

On the fifteenth day Krishna argued that Drona could not be beaten in fair fight, only broken by grief. Bhima killed an elephant named Ashvatthama and shouted that Ashvatthama was dead. Drona turned to Yudhishthira, who was known never to lie. Yudhishthira confirmed it and spoke the words 'the elephant' so that Drona did not catch them. The epic says that Yudhishthira's chariot, which had always run a little above the ground, touched the earth at that moment.

Drona laid down his weapons and sat in meditation. Dhrishtadyumna, born from Drupada's sacrifice to kill him, struck him down there, while Arjuna shouted to take the teacher alive. The victory was real, and so was the doubt it left: Arjuna and others reproached Dhrishtadyumna, and Ashvatthama's grief at his father's death would return as the night raid.

chapters.title: Abhimanyu in the Chakravyuha
chapters.subtitle: Day thirteen: the wheel array and the breach that closed
narrative: On the thirteenth day Drona arranged his forces in the chakravyuha, the wheel or circular array, while the Samshaptakas kept Arjuna and Krishna busy far away. Of those left in the Pandava camp, only Arjuna's son Abhimanyu claimed to know how to break into it. He told Yudhishthira plainly that he knew the way in but not the way out. The others promised to follow through the breach he made.

He broke in. Behind him, Jayadratha, king of the Sindhus, held the gap shut. The epic says Shiva had granted him the power to hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for a single day, a boon he had won after his humiliation in the forest years before. Bhima, Yudhishthira, the twins and their allies were stopped at the edge of the wheel while Abhimanyu fought on alone inside.

The epic gives him a long and brilliant fight before the great warriors of the Kaurava side turned on him together. On Drona's advice Karna cut his bow from behind, while others killed his horses and charioteer. He fought on with a sword and then a chariot wheel, and finally, in a mace fight, Dushasana's son struck him as he rose. His young wife Uttara was pregnant with Parikshit, the child through whom the Kuru line would survive.

Many retellings add that Abhimanyu learned to enter the array while still in his mother's womb, overhearing Arjuna describe it to Subhadra, and that Subhadra fell asleep before he explained the exit. That story is widely loved and widely told in later and regional versions; the epic's own account simply has Abhimanyu say what he knew and what he did not.

The epic names a group of great chariot-warriors who surround Abhimanyu together (often counted as six, including Drona, Kripa, Karna, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma), but many more attack him over the course of the day, and retellings vary the names and the order of the blows.

chapters.title: Karna's Final Battle
chapters.subtitle: Days sixteen and seventeen: the eldest son of Kunti fights for the other side
narrative: With Drona dead, Duryodhana gave command to Karna, his friend since the tournament where Karna had been mocked as a charioteer's son. Karna asked for a charioteer worthy of facing Krishna and named Shalya, king of the Madras and maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva. Shalya was furious to be asked to drive for a man he called a charioteer's son, and he agreed only if he could say what he liked. The epic adds that he had already promised Yudhishthira that he would wear down Karna's spirit, and he spent the ride doing exactly that.

These were days of debts coming due. Over the course of the war Karna had Bhima, Sahadeva, Nakula and finally Yudhishthira at his mercy at different moments and let each of them go, keeping his promise to Kunti that she would still have five sons when the war was over. Wounded and humiliated, Yudhishthira told Arjuna he should hand the Gandiva to someone worthier. Arjuna, bound by a private vow to kill anyone who said that, reached for his sword until Krishna talked both brothers back from the edge. On the seventeenth day Bhima found Dushasana and kept the terrible vow he had made in the dice hall when Draupadi was dragged before the court.

Then the duel. Karna loosed an arrow carrying the serpent Ashvasena, who had his own grudge against Arjuna from the burning of the Khandava forest. Krishna pressed the chariot down into the earth so that the arrow took only Arjuna's crown. Later Karna's chariot wheel sank into the ground, as a brahmin's curse had foretold, and the divine weapon Parashurama taught him slipped from his memory, as that teacher's curse had said it would. Karna climbed down and asked Arjuna to wait, invoking the rules of fair fight. Krishna answered by listing the dice hall, Draupadi and Abhimanyu: where had Karna's dharma been then? Arjuna shot.

Only after the war would Kunti tell her sons that the man they killed was their eldest brother. Modern novels, plays and films have made Karna the epic's great tragic hero, and that reading has real grounding in his generosity and his loyalty. But the epic's own portrait is mixed. It also remembers his cruelty to Draupadi in the dice hall.

chapters.title: The End of the War
chapters.subtitle: Day eighteen, the broken king, and the mothers on the field
narrative: On the eighteenth day Shalya led what was left of the Kaurava army, and Yudhishthira, the least warlike of the brothers, killed him. Sahadeva killed Shakuni, the dice player whose game had begun it all. By afternoon the great host had melted away, and Duryodhana, alone and on foot, hid beneath the waters of a lake. When the Pandavas found him, Yudhishthira offered him the kingdom if he could beat any one of them in single combat, with any weapon he liked. Krishna rebuked him for staking everything on a single throw once again.

Duryodhana chose the mace and chose Bhima. Balarama, who had taught both of them and had stayed out of the war on pilgrimage, arrived to watch. The fight was even until Krishna remarked to Arjuna that Bhima could not win by the rules. Arjuna struck his own thigh as a signal, and Bhima broke Duryodhana's thighs, fulfilling the vow he had sworn in the dice hall. A blow below the navel was forbidden, and Balarama, enraged, had to be restrained by Krishna.

Lying broken, Duryodhana named each trick by which the Pandavas had won and claimed he had lived as a king should. The epic says flowers fell on him from the sky. Victory belonged to the Pandavas, but the text lets the defeated man speak and lets heaven seem to honour him, an honesty that has troubled and fascinated readers ever since.

Then came the night raid, and after it the women. In the Stri Parva Gandhari, given sight of the field by Vyasa, walked among the dead with the widows of both armies. Grief turned her toward Krishna, who could have stopped the war, and she cursed him and his Yadava clan to destroy one another in thirty-six years. Krishna accepted it calmly. At the funeral offerings by the Ganga, Kunti finally told her sons that Karna had been their eldest brother.

chapters.title: The Night Raid
chapters.subtitle: Sauptika: the massacre of the sleeping camp and the weapon aimed at the unborn
narrative: On the night after the mace duel, the three Kaurava survivors, Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma, rested beneath a great tree. Ashvatthama lay awake and watched an owl fall on a tree full of sleeping crows and kill them one by one. He took it as instruction. Kripa argued that killing sleeping men was against every law of war and urged him to ask the elders for counsel first; Ashvatthama would not wait.

At the gate of the Pandava camp the epic sets a terrifying guardian, and Ashvatthama offers himself up to Shiva, who gives him a sword and enters him. Inside the camp he killed Dhrishtadyumna, his father's slayer, without a weapon, denying him a warrior's death, and then Shikhandi, Draupadi's five sons and many others as they woke in confusion. Kripa and Kritavarma cut down those who fled through the gate. The five Pandavas, Krishna and Satyaki survived only because they were spending the night away from the camp. Ashvatthama carried the news to Duryodhana, who died content.

Draupadi, who had lost all her sons in one night, vowed to fast until Ashvatthama was punished. Bhima went after him, with Krishna, Arjuna and Yudhishthira following, and found him beside the Ganga among sages near Vyasa. Cornered, Ashvatthama released the Brahmashira weapon; Arjuna released his own to counter it. Vyasa and Narada stood between the two fires. Arjuna was able to withdraw his weapon, but Ashvatthama could not, and he turned it on the wombs of the Pandava women, where Uttara carried Abhimanyu's son.

Krishna promised to revive the child and cursed Ashvatthama to wander the earth for three thousand years, sick and shunned. Ashvatthama gave up the gem he wore on his forehead, and Draupadi accepted it in place of his life. Later traditions remember Ashvatthama as one of the long-lived immortals (chiranjivi), and regional legends place sightings of him far from the epic's own pages.

chapters.title: The Return to Hastinapura
chapters.subtitle: A crown no one wants, a dying grandfather's counsel, and the long work of repair
narrative: After the funeral rites, while the Pandavas stayed a month by the Ganga in mourning, Yudhishthira found that he did not want the throne. At the start of the Shanti Parva he tells his brothers he will go to the forest as a renunciant, since the kingdom was bought with the lives of kinsmen, teachers and his own unrecognised brother. Arjuna, Bhima, the twins and Draupadi argue fiercely that a king who abandons his people after such a war only adds to the harm. Vyasa and Krishna add their weight, and at last he enters Hastinapura and accepts the crown, with old Dhritarashtra still honoured in the palace.

Krishna then takes him to Kurukshetra, where Bhishma still lies on his bed of arrows, waiting for the sun's northward turn to choose his death. What follows is among the longest stretches of the whole epic: Bhishma's teachings on the duties of kings (rajadharma), on conduct in times of disaster (apaddharma) and on liberation (mokshadharma), continuing into the Anushasana Parva. Tradition also places the Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu, in this setting. When the sun turned, Bhishma gave up his life.

Recovery is shown as ritual and as labour. Vyasa urges a horse sacrifice (ashvamedha), and Arjuna follows the wandering horse across the kingdoms; in Manipura he is killed in battle by his own son Babhruvahana and revived by the Naga princess Ulupi. Abhimanyu's son Parikshit is born lifeless and restored by Krishna, as promised on the morning after the night raid. At the end of the sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, appears and declares the whole lavish rite worth less than a poor family's gift of a little flour to a hungry guest.

Fifteen years later Dhritarashtra and Gandhari leave for the forest, and Kunti, to her sons' dismay, goes with them; Vidura and Sanjaya follow. Vidura dies in the forest. Vyasa, the epic says, called the fallen warriors up from the Ganga for a single night so that the living could see them again. Some time afterwards a forest fire took the three elders, and Sanjaya went on alone to the Himalaya.

chapters.title: The Fall of Dwaraka
chapters.subtitle: Mausala: thirty-six years after the war, the curse comes due
narrative: Thirty-six years after the war, as Gandhari had said, the omens gathered over Dwaraka. Some young Yadavas dressed Krishna's son Samba as a pregnant woman and asked visiting sages what child she would bear. The sages answered with a curse: she would bring forth an iron club (musala) that would destroy the clan. The club appeared; it was ground to powder and thrown into the sea, and the city's elders banned strong drink. None of it helped.

On a pilgrimage to Prabhasa by the sea, the Yadavas drank. Old wounds opened: Satyaki mocked Kritavarma for joining the night raid on sleeping men, and the quarrel became a slaughter in which kinsmen killed one another with stalks of eraka grass that turned into clubs in their hands. Many retellings say the grass grew from the powdered club, a link drawn most vividly in later Puranic tellings. The war that had ended at Kurukshetra finished its work among the people who had won it.

Balarama sat in meditation by the shore and left his body; the epic describes a great serpent issuing from his mouth into the sea. Krishna withdrew into the forest and lay down in yoga, and a hunter named Jara, mistaking his foot for a deer, shot him. The epic tells this with striking restraint: the god who drove Arjuna's chariot dies by a stranger's error, as the curses had foretold.

Summoned by Krishna's charioteer, Arjuna came to an emptied city, performed the funeral rites and led its women, children and old people away. Behind them the sea came in over Dwaraka. On the road, herdsmen-robbers attacked the convoy, and Arjuna could barely string the Gandiva; his divine weapons would not come to mind. Vyasa told him that the time for those powers had passed. This is what the Pandavas hear before they set out on their final journey.

story_context.sources_note: The Mausala Parva is short and stark. Later works such as the Bhagavata Purana and the Vishnu Purana tell the end of the Yadavas at greater length and with devotional emphasis (including the powdered club growing into the eraka grass and a fragment becoming the hunter's arrowhead), and popular retellings often combine their details with the epic's. Dwaraka is traditionally identified with Dwarka on the Gujarat coast; modern underwater surveys there are separate from the epic's narrative and their interpretation remains debated.

chapters.title: The Final Journey
chapters.subtitle: Mahaprasthana and Svargarohana: the walk into the mountains and the last test
narrative: When Arjuna returned with the news of Dwaraka, Yudhishthira understood that their time was over too. He crowned Parikshit in Hastinapura, set Krishna's great-grandson Vajra over Indraprastha, and with his brothers and Draupadi put on bark garments and walked out of the city. A dog followed them. On the shore of the eastern sea the fire god Agni appeared and asked Arjuna to give the Gandiva back to the waters. The bow that had decided the war went into the sea.

They circled the land and turned north into the Himalaya, Yudhishthira walking in front. Draupadi fell first, and when Bhima asked why, Yudhishthira said she had loved Arjuna more than the rest. Sahadeva fell next for pride in his wisdom, Nakula for pride in his beauty, Arjuna for boasting he would destroy every enemy in a single day, and Bhima for appetite and pride in his strength. Each time Yudhishthira gave his reason and walked on without looking back. The epic does not ask us to find this comforting.

Indra came down in his chariot to carry Yudhishthira to heaven in his own body, but told him the dog could not come. Yudhishthira refused to abandon a creature that had been loyal to him, even for heaven. The dog then revealed itself as Dharma, Yudhishthira's divine father, who had tested him before at the lake in the forest. In heaven Yudhishthira found Duryodhana enthroned and his own brothers missing. Led to a dark and stinking place where he heard the voices of Karna, his brothers and Draupadi begging him to stay, he chose to remain with them. The scene dissolved: it had been an illusion, Indra said, a brief experience of hell owed for his deception of Drona.

Yudhishthira bathed in the heavenly Ganga, left his human body, and found each of the dead restored to the divine source the epic assigns them. Then the story folds back to where it began: Vaishampayana finishes his recitation at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice, and Ugrashravas, the bard, finishes telling it to the sages in the Naimisha forest.

story_context.sources_note: The reasons given for each fall are Yudhishthira's own judgements in the text, and commentators have long debated them, especially the charge against Draupadi. The two final books are short and are sometimes read as a later or separately shaped conclusion. The route around the land and up to Mount Meru is described in the epic's own sacred geography, not as a mapped itinerary.

central_question.deeper_context: The Pandavas give up the kingdom, the bow and finally their bodies. Yudhishthira's last tests are about refusing to let go of loyalty while letting go of everything else.

questions.question: Is Yudhishthira's verdict on each fallen companion just, or is it the last of his blind spots?
questions.deeper_context: He blames Draupadi for loving Arjuna most, but says nothing about the dice game in which he staked her. Readers have long asked whether the epic endorses his judgements or lets us see past them.

questions.question: Why is refusing heaven for a dog the act that proves Yudhishthira worthy?
questions.deeper_context: After walking past the bodies of his wife and brothers, he will not abandon a dog. The epic frames this as loyalty to one who depends on you, and Dharma's appearance links it to the questions at the lake in the forest years before.

questions.question: Duryodhana in heaven, the Pandavas in hell: what kind of justice is the epic's last illusion?
questions.deeper_context: Yudhishthira is outraged to see Duryodhana honoured for dying as a warrior should. He chooses hell to be with his family, and only then is the illusion lifted. The ending refuses to make merit simple or to let the victor's view stand unexamined.

questions.question: Why does the epic end not in heaven but with someone listening?
